segments.heading: Documentation text: what the script is
segments.text:
- Lines 2 to 78 are the documentation text of the script. Python does not execute it. `main` prints it when it finds too many arguments or an unknown option (line 293).
- The script accepts or rejects a build of the runner program `bwx12`. Its input is the machine code of every kernel, as text.
- Line 3 cites the design rule that a build is rejected when its acceptance listing differs [Ref8].
- `check_listing11.py` is the script of the same kind in the folder of `bwx11`, the runner version before `bwx12`.

- The script runs on the development machine, not on CRB.
- It reads `listing.txt` and `offsets.tsv`. The script `build12.sh` wrote both files on CRB [Ref6].
- Both file arguments are optional. Lines 295 and 296 set the defaults.
- The reference is a saved copy of the same two files from the accepted build of `bwx11`. The copies are equal, byte for byte, to the files in the build folder of `bwx11` [Ref3].

segments.heading: Documentation text: part 1, the 29 kernels of the reference
segments.text:
Part 1 covers the kernels that `bwx11` already had. Five of the six kernels of the whole-chip test are among them: `oldread`, `read`, `asmread`, `read_nop96` and `read_1pl`.
- Rule 1: lines 321 to 325.
- Rule 2: lines 327 to 330.
- Rule 3: lines 339 and 340.
- Rule 4: lines 341 to 344.
"Loop start modulo 64" is the remainder of the loop start address divided by 64.

These lines define how two functions at different addresses are compared. The function `whole` (line 181) implements it.
- `bl` is the call instruction. The listing has 2 `bl` instructions, one in `oldread` and one in `oldread2`. Both call `__stack_chk_fail@plt`, the function for a failed stack guard [Ref2].
- `adrp` puts the address of a 4096-byte page into a register. The `ldr` after it loads a pointer from that page.
- The "table of global addresses" holds addresses of global objects of the binary. The linker sets the page and the offset of an entry. So the script does not compare them with the reference.
- Lines 43 and 44 define the loop. The function `loop_start` (line 171) finds its first address.

segments.heading: Documentation text: part 2, the 26 new kernels
segments.text:
Part 2 covers the kernels that `bwx12` adds to `bwx11`. The whole-chip test runs one of them: `read_nop256`. The function `new_problems` (line 208) implements the five rules.
- "Round 5" is the name in `bwx12.c` for these 26 additions [Ref7]. It is not a round of a kernel sequence.
- Rule 1: lines 214 to 225.
- Rule 2: lines 226 to 238. Lines 91 to 131 build the expected lists.
- `ldp` loads a pair of registers. `stp` stores a pair. `nop` does nothing.
- `b.cc` and `b.lo` are two names of one branch instruction. After `cmp x0, x1` it jumps when `x0` is below `x1` (unsigned compare).

- Rule 3: lines 239 to 259.
- Rule 4: lines 260 to 265. A callee-saved register must hold the same value when the function returns as when it was called. A kernel whose loop loads into q8 to q15 must store d8 to d15 before the loop and reload them after it.
- Rule 5: lines 266 to 273.
- Line 72 is implemented in lines 357 to 360.

- `--skip-new` was not used for the accepted build of `bwx12`. The summary line of the saved output says `new_kernels=26`, not `NOT CHECKED` [Ref1].
- The exit status is the return value of `main` (line 394).

- `HERE` is the folder of this script. `REF_DIR` is its subfolder `ref-bwx11`.
- `TARGET` is a text pattern for a branch target at the end of an instruction: a hexadecimal address, a space and a name in angle brackets. Example: `49a4 <k_read+0x4>`. The pattern captures the address. The page operand of an `adrp` instruction has the same form. The pattern matches it too. Example: `2f000 <__FRAME_END__+0x16a34>`.

segments.heading: Expected instruction lists of the new kernels
segments.text:
The lists hold instruction text in the form that the function `sections` (line 138) produces: one space between the fields.
- `LDP8`: the 8 `ldp` instructions of `asmread`. Each one loads two 16-byte registers. Together they load q0 to q15 from the 256 bytes at the pointer `x0`.
- `STEP`: add 256 bytes (`#0x100`) to `x0`, then compare `x0` with the end pointer `x1`. `STEP128` adds 128 bytes (`#0x80`).
- `LDR4`: 4 `ldr` instructions. Each one loads 16 bytes. The offsets from `x0` are 0, 64, 128 and 192 bytes.

- `STP8`: 8 `stp` instructions. Each one stores q0 twice (32 bytes). The offsets from `x0` are 0, 32 and so on up to 224 bytes.
- `COPY_LDP8`: `LDP8` with the source pointer `x1`. `COPY_STP8`: 8 `stp` that store q0 to q15 at the destination pointer `x0`.
- `COPY_STEP`: add 256 bytes to both pointers, then compare the source pointer with the end pointer `x2`.
- `END_POINTER`: the instruction before the loop that computes the end address: pointer plus 8 times the second argument. The second argument of a kernel is a count of 8-byte words [Ref9]. `lsl #3` shifts it left by 3 bits.
- `COPY_END_POINTER`: the same instruction with the registers of a copy kernel.
- `ACC_ZERO`: 8 `movi` that set v16 to v23 to zero. `CONST_ONE`: 8 `movi` that set each 32-bit lane of v24 to v31 to 1.

segments.heading: Functions `vadd` and `spec`: build one expectation
segments.text:
- `vadd` turns pairs of register numbers (a, b) into the instruction texts `add va.2d, va.2d, vb.2d`. This instruction adds the two 64-bit lanes of register b to register a.
- `spec` returns the expectation of one new kernel as a dictionary with 5 fields.
- `loop`: the loop instructions without the loop branch. `mod`: the planned loop start modulo 64.
- `like`: the older kernel that must have the same loop start modulo 64 in the same listing.
- `init`: the extra instructions before the loop. `end`: the end-pointer instruction.

segments.heading: Table `NEW`: the 26 new kernels and their expected loops
segments.text:
- Lines 118 and 119: 9 kernels `read_nopN`. The loop is `LDP8`, N `nop`, `STEP`. The whole-chip test runs `read_nop256` (N = 256).
- Lines 120 to 123: `read_dadd2` to `read_dadd16`. After the loads come 2 to 16 vector adds. Each add takes a register that the loads of the same loop pass filled.
- Line 124: `read_iadd16`. Its 16 adds take the constant registers v24 to v31, not a loaded register.
- Lines 125 to 127: 5 kernels `read_spN` (4 `ldp`, 128 bytes per loop pass, N `nop`) and `read_1pl_nop96` (`LDR4`, 96 `nop`).
- Lines 128 to 131: 4 write kernels (planned loop start modulo 64: 40 bytes, original `asmwrite`) and 2 copy kernels (planned 52 bytes, original `asmcopy`). Every read kernel has the planned value 20 bytes and the original `asmread`.
- Line 132: `NEW_LOOP` is a second name for the same table.

- `SAVE` matches a store of one or two d registers to the stack, for example `stp d8, d9, [sp, #-64]!`. It captures the register numbers.
- `RESTORE` matches a load of one or two d registers from the stack, for example `ldp d8, d9, [sp], #64`.
- `BRANCH` matches the name of a branch or call instruction at the start of the text: `b`, `bl`, `br`, `blr`, a conditional `b.xx`, `cbz`, `cbnz`, `tbz`, `tbnz`. It does not match `ret`.

segments.heading: Function `sections`: read a listing file
segments.text:
Returns a dictionary. The key is the pair (binary, kernel). The value is the list of (address, instruction text) of that kernel function, in file order.
- Lines 143 to 146: a line such as `=== bwx12 read ===` starts the block of one kernel.
- Line 147: an instruction line holds a hexadecimal address, a colon and the instruction. The function header `00000000000049a0 <k_read>:` does not match and is skipped.
- Line 149: the objdump comment after `//` is cut off. Each run of spaces and tabs becomes one space.
- Lines 151 and 152: a line that starts with `##` ends the current block.

segments.heading: Function `offsets`: read offsets.tsv
segments.text:
Returns a dictionary from (binary, kernel) to the text of column 6, `loop_mod64`.
- Lines 160 to 162: the first line must hold exactly the 6 column names, separated by tab characters.
- Lines 163 to 166: every other line must have 6 fields.
- A wrong header or row raises `ValueError`. `main` then ends with exit status 2 (lines 300 to 302).
- The script uses columns 1, 2 and 6 only. It ignores the columns `function`, `start` and `loop_start`.

segments.heading: Function `loop_start`: first address of the loop
segments.text:
- Goes through the instructions in order. It returns the target of the first branch whose target lies inside the function and before the branch itself (`first <= target < addr`). This address is the loop start.
- It returns `None` when the function has no such branch.
- `main` computes every loop start modulo 64 of part 1 as `loop_start(...) % 64`.

segments.heading: Function `whole`: function text without addresses
segments.text:
Returns two lists: the instruction texts without addresses (`out`), and the places of the pointer loads from the table of global addresses (`got`).
- Lines 188 and 189: a branch target inside the function becomes its distance from the function start. Example: `b.hi 49a4 <k_read+0x4>` becomes `b.hi +0x4`.
- Lines 190 to 192: a target outside the function becomes `(outside <name>)`. The name is kept. The address is removed. Example: `bl (outside <__stack_chk_fail@plt>)`. `page` keeps the address text for line 199.

These lines handle the pair `adrp xN, page` and `ldr xN, [xN, #offset]` with one register xN.
- Line 195 records the place (page, offset) in `got`.
- Lines 196 and 197 replace both texts by fixed texts: `adrp xN, (table page)` and `ldr xN, [xN, #(table)]`. So page and offset are not part of the text comparison.
- Lines 198 and 199 remember the register and the page of an `adrp` for the next instruction only.
In both listings only `oldread` and `oldread2` have this pair. Each has it twice, with the page address `2f000` (hexadecimal) and the offset 4072 bytes [Ref2] [Ref3].

segments.heading: Function `numbers`: register numbers of one match
segments.text: Returns the set of register numbers that one `SAVE` or `RESTORE` match captured.

segments.heading: Function `new_problems`: the five rules of part 2
segments.text:
Returns a list of problem texts for one new kernel. An empty list says that the kernel passed.
- Lines 214 to 217: `back` lists every instruction that has a branch target inside the function, at or before its own address. Exactly 1 is required. If not, the function returns immediately with this one problem.
- Lines 218 to 222: `end` is the index of that branch. `loop` is its target address. `begin` is the index of the instruction at that address. If no instruction has that address, the function returns with one problem.
- Lines 223 to 225 (rule 1): any other instruction that `BRANCH` matches is a problem. The `ret` at the end is not a problem.

Rule 2.
- Line 226: `body` is the instruction text from the loop start to the instruction before the loop branch. `want` is the expected list from `NEW`.
- Line 227: the two lists must be equal. So the count, the order, and every register and offset of the loop instructions are compared.
- Lines 228 to 236 only write the messages: the `nop` count if it differs, the first 3 differing instructions, and the number of further ones.
- Lines 237 and 238: the loop branch must be `b.cc` or `b.lo`. The name after its target address must be `k_` plus the kernel name, plus the distance of the loop start from the function start.

Rule 3, before the loop. `head` holds the instructions before the loop start. `tail` holds the instructions after the loop branch.
- Lines 241 to 246: an instruction that `SAVE` matches adds its register numbers to `saved`. Every other instruction, apart from the end-pointer instruction, is added to the list `init`.
- Lines 247 and 248: the end-pointer instruction must occur exactly 1 time.
- Lines 249 to 251: `init` must equal the field `init` of the expectation, in the same order. For `read_nop256` this field is empty. So only stores of d registers and the end-pointer instruction may stand before its loop.

Rule 3, after the loop, and rule 4.
- Lines 252 to 259: the last instruction must be `ret`. Every instruction between the loop branch and `ret` must be a load that `RESTORE` matches.
- Line 260: `used` holds the register numbers 8 to 15 that the loop names as a q, v or d register.
- Lines 261 to 263: every register in `used` must be in `saved` and in `restored`.
- Lines 264 and 265: the stored set and the reloaded set must be equal.
- The script compares register numbers only. It does not compare the stack offset of a store with the stack offset of its reload.

Rule 5, the place of the loop. `loop % 64` is the loop start modulo 64 of this kernel.
- Lines 266 to 269: it must equal `want_mod`, the value of the original kernel (field `like`) in the same listing. `main` computes `want_mod` in lines 367 to 371 and line 375. When the original kernel has no loop in the listing, `want_mod` is `None`. This is also a problem.
- Lines 270 and 271: it must equal the planned value of `NEW`.
- Lines 272 and 273: the row of the kernel in `offsets.tsv` must hold the same number.

segments.heading: Function `main`: arguments
segments.text:
- Lines 279 and 280: the defaults of the 4 options. The reference files are in `ref-bwx11`. The binary name is `bwx12`. The reference binary name is `bwx11`.
- Lines 281 to 283: `--skip-new` is a flag without a value.
- Lines 284 to 291: an option that is present takes the next argument as its value. Both are removed from the list. An option without a value ends the script with exit status 2.
- Lines 292 to 294: more than 2 remaining arguments, or a remaining argument that starts with `--`, print the documentation text. The script then ends with exit status 2.

segments.heading: Function `main`: read the files, refuse unusable input
segments.text:
- Lines 295 and 296: the listing is the first argument, or `listing.txt` in the folder of the script. The offsets table is the second argument, or `offsets.tsv` in the folder of the listing.
- Lines 297 to 302: read the reference listing (`ref`), the new listing (`got`) and the two offsets tables. A file that cannot be opened, or an offsets table with a wrong form, ends the script with exit status 2.
- Line 304: `kernels` lists the kernel names of the reference binary, in the order of the reference listing.
- Lines 305 to 313: three more cases end with exit status 2. Case 1: the reference listing has no kernel of the reference binary, or a reference kernel has no instructions or no loop. Case 2: the reference holds a kernel of `NEW`. Case 3: the new listing has no block of the binary `bwx12`.

segments.heading: Part 1: one output row per kernel of the reference
segments.text:
- Line 317 prints the column names of the first output table.
- Line 320: `r_mod` is the loop start modulo 64 of the kernel in the reference listing.
- Lines 321 to 325 (rule 1): the new listing must have a block for the kernel, and the function must have a backward branch. If not, the row says `FAIL: no listing or no loop`.
- `bad` counts the failures of part 1.

Rule 2, the function text.
- Lines 327 and 328: `whole` (line 181) gives the text without addresses of the reference function and of the new function. `same` is true when the two lists are equal: the same number of instructions, and each instruction text equal with every operand.
- Lines 329 and 330: unequal text is a problem.
- Lines 332 to 336: `r_got` and `g_got` are the places of the pointer loads from the table of global addresses. More distinct places in the new function than in the reference function is a problem.
- Lines 337 and 338: a new function with no more places than the reference, but with other offsets, gets a note and not a failure. When the row has no failure, its result column then starts with `NOTE: got_offset_differs` in place of `ok`. No row of the accepted build of `bwx12` has this note [Ref1].

Rules 3 and 4, then the output row.
- Lines 339 and 340: the loop start modulo 64 of the new listing must equal the reference value.
- Lines 341 and 342: the reference `offsets.tsv` must hold the reference value.
- Lines 343 and 344: the new `offsets.tsv` must hold the value of the new listing.
- Lines 345 and 346 print the row: kernel, function start and loop start (hexadecimal addresses), loop start modulo 64, reference value, `same` or `DIFFERS`, and the result `ok`, `NOTE: ...` or `FAIL: ...`.
- Lines 347 to 351: when the text differs, both texts are printed side by side. `!=` marks a line that differs.

Two checks over all kernels of part 1. Each failure adds 1 to `bad`.
- Lines 353 to 356: the places are collected over all kernels with equal text. The new listing may not use more distinct places of the table of global addresses than the reference.
- Lines 357 to 360: a kernel of `bwx12` in the new listing is a failure when it is not in the reference and not in `NEW`.

segments.heading: Part 2: one output row per new kernel
segments.text:
- Lines 364 to 366: with `--skip-new` the script prints the summary line here and returns. The new kernels are then not checked.
- Lines 367 to 371: `like_mod` holds the loop start modulo 64 of `asmcopy`, `asmread` and `asmwrite` in the new listing. These are the three originals that `NEW` names. A value is `None` when the kernel is missing or has no loop.

- Line 372 prints the column names of the second output table.
- Lines 373 to 379: every kernel of `NEW` must have a block in the new listing. If not, the row says `FAIL: no listing`.
- Line 380: `new_problems` (line 208) applies the five rules.
- Lines 382 to 386 print the row: kernel, function start, loop start, loop start modulo 64, the value of the original kernel, `expected` or `DIFFERS`, and the result `ok` or `FAIL: ...`.
- The sixth column says `DIFFERS` when a problem text is about the loop instructions, the `nop` count, the loop branch, another branch or call, or the number of backward branches. Any other problem shows only in the result column.

- Lines 388 and 389 print the summary line. For the accepted build of `bwx12` it is `# binary=bwx12 reference=bwx11 kernels=29 failed_rows=0 new_kernels=26 new_failed_rows=0` [Ref1].
- Line 390: `main` returns 1 when a check of part 1 or part 2 failed, and 0 when none failed.
- Line 394 makes this value the exit status of the script.
